processing: Stems of high-grade tea, sorted out from gyokuro or sencha refining, are roasted. Methods differ by maker: pan-roasting over high heat, or a two-stage oven and sand roast.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking; the stems come from refining and are roasted later.
appearance_dry: Light to mid-brown roasted stems, some still with a greenish core.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber to golden brown, depending on roast.
taste_profile: Deeply sweet and toasty, with a nutty, almond-like warmth and very little bitterness; lighter roasts stay smoother and more delicate.

brewing.notes: Unlike the green karigane, this one wants near-boiling water. Short steeps keep it sweet; it also works well cold.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage. Merchants roast through the year and sell it as a current product, and the toasted aroma fades, so buy small and drink within months of opening. Grades reflect the stem quality and the roast.
description:
Take the good stems sorted out of gyokuro or fine sencha and roast them, and you get a hojicha that is noticeably sweeter and rounder than the everyday kind. That is the whole idea of karigane hojicha: the same familiar toasty cup, built on better raw material.

Roasting style matters as much as the stems. Some makers pan-roast over high heat; others go twice, first in an oven and then in hot sand. Lighter versions exist too, gentler and smoother.

Expect sweetness first, then roast, with an almond-like or nutty warmth. Sellers link the sweetness to the theanine in stems. Use very hot water and short steeps, and do not over-leaf it.

This tea appears from several regions, including Uji and Shiga, so check the origin and what the stems are from. It suits the evening, since roasted stem tea is typically low in caffeine.
history: Little is documented about the origin of this style as a named tea. Hojicha roasting and the sale of refining stems as karigane are both established, and this tea combines the two; today it appears mainly as a speciality of individual merchants, each with a roasting method of its own.
